entry.title: Meet Prometheus, a Gift Link Search Engine
entry.summary:
Sometime in the past few years, media sites like Bloomberg, The Economist, The Atlantic, Defector, Talking Points Memo, and the NY Times started offering a way for subscribers to share paywalled articles with friends and followers. These are commonly referred to as gift links. Thousands of gift links are shared on websites and social media daily. Some helpful aggregated feeds and hashtags are available, but finding specific information can be difficult. Whenever possible here on KDO, I link to paywalled articles with gift links. To help in that endeavor, I’ve built a gift link discovery tool called Prometheus. Prometheus collects gift links to paywalled news articles shared by subscribers — from the New York Times, the Washington Post, the Atlantic, and more. Links are gathered from Bluesky, Mastodon, and the web throughout the day, and you can search by keyword & URL and filter by publication.
Right now, Prometheus is only available to active kottke.org members while I’m testing and refining it — it’s definitely a beta tool rn. If you’re a member, check it out and let me know if you’ve got any feedback or notice any rough edges. An informed public is the foundation of a healthy society — and while paywalls aren’t the only challenge here, they also aren’t helping. Big thanks to everyone sharing their gift links online and to these media companies for enabling their subscribers to share their journalism with others.

entry.title: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security
entry.summary:
Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security

If you're running anything on PHP it's vital you upgrade - today's updates (across the entire PHP 8.x line) address two remote code execution holes, and there have been exploits circulating since last night, thanks to a leak in the coordinated disclosure process.

This post from the PHP Foundation explain what went so wrong:

On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC. It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...]

As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st.

This article from the team that discovered the original vulnerability includes a more detailed timeline of the original intended responsible disclosure:

  • August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol.
  • August 20, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against Drupal.
  • August 21, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against WordPress.
  • August 24, 2026: Wiz Research reports the vulnerabilities to the PHP security team.
  • September 21, 2026: PHP acknowledges the reports and begins developing a coordinated fix.
  • October 21, 2026: Patched PHP releases become available.
  • October 21, 2026: Public disclosure.

Via Hacker News

Ambient Earth is a 7.5-hour, real-time, 4K, remastered video of the orbital view from the International Space Station. Seán Doran took almost 49,000 images from 27 time-lapse sequences captured from the ISS by astronaut Butch Wilmore, repaired, remastered, and interpolated them into this incredible video. Perspective is lost when the world speeds by. The scale and beauty of our home planet is truly appreciated when observed on an epic 7.5 hour journey from The International Space Station. This ambitious 4k compilation, crafted through months of meticulous restoration, invites you to slow down and experience Earth in real time just as astronauts do.
The video is accompanied by ambient audio recorded on the station by Chris Hadfield. This would be great for a screensaver, but after poking around for a bit, it doesn’t seem like there’s a good way to set a YT video as a screensaver on MacOS (without downloading it or having it be a livestream).

entry.summary:
eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise

This is very, very bad news:

The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised. They chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores.

Any software that bundles a list of trusted certificates needs to be updated. This site is tracking software updates via this GitHub repository - Linux distros need to update their ca-certificates packages.

In Python world uv 0.13.4 and pip 26.2.2 and certifi 2026.10.19 have been released with upgraded certificate lists.

entry.title: Battle Drones - a vibe coded RTS with audio-based multiplayer
entry.summary:
My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones (play it here). Unlike my previous experiments, this one is actually fun to play. I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to "Make it a LOT more fun". It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here's what I've built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way.

  • Battle Drones
  • How I built this
  • v1: the initial prototype
  • v2: full sprites
  • v3: varied terrain
  • v4: the fun update
  • v5: Battle Drones goes 3D
  • v8: Archipelago
  • v10: Goliath, and agent battles
  • Agent battles
  • v11: Random Maps
  • v12: Multiplayer via sound
  • Some thoughts

Battle Drones

My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer. I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic.

After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other.

Here's a video demo of Battle Drones running in a desktop browser:

Features so far include:

  • 9 buildings, 7 ground vehicles, 6 aerial vehicles, 3 infantry units - all 3D models, which you can browse here
  • Fog of war
  • Different weapons are needed to target aerial or ground vehicles
  • Six maps, across five biomes - temperate, desert, arctic, volcanic, tropical
  • A random map generator
  • Skirmish mode - red vs. blue on a rotationally symmetrical map
  • Last Stand mode - one player holds out against as many waves of enemies as possible
  • Area effect weapons: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod, Sky Hammer
  • Crate drops with bonus resources
  • In-game music that responds to events - it gets more intense as fighting breaks out
  • Different in-game AI personalities (Balanced, Rush, Air Swarm, Boom, Skyforce, Ironclad)
  • AI vs. AI mode, to watch those personalities play each other
  • The Goliath - a giant stomping mech with laser eyes and arm cannons and the ability to establish a new base
  • Mutators that add extra rules or twists
  • A "Daily Op" challenge
  • Ranks and achievements (Medals)
  • Agent vs. Agent mode where two LLMs can play Battle Drones against each other
  • A multiplayer mode based on two nearby phones communicating via audio messages, an extension of my earlier experiment with Chirp Pong

How I built this

Battle Drones is heavily vibe coded - I've reviewed almost none of the code, and it's built in a language (TypeScript) that I've hardly used myself. I've playtested it quite a bit though, and it's been through a large number of iterations since I started the project.

Here's a rough history of the project so far, including key prompts and links to transcripts.

v1: the initial prototype

I started out with Claude Fable 5 back in July:

We are going to build a mobile friendly RTS game - command and conquer style - called Battle Drones, in which two armies of drones (both flying and ground-based) battle for territory and resources

Let's start with a MVP design, ask me some questions

Here's a shared transcript. I'd given Claude Code for Web an environment variable with an OpenAI API key and told it to use the OpenAI Image Generation API for assets, which got me some basic sprites.

You can try v1 here - it looked like this:

It's recognizable as an RTS, has building mechanics and the ability to select and direct units, and a basic AI to play against.

This first version was barely a proof of concept, and it wasn't any fun to play.

Claude used the Phaser 2D game framework for these early versions. I didn't even realize this until several iterations later!

v2: full sprites

The second version (try v2 here) added sprites for all of the vehicles and the "AI vs. AI" mode, so I could watch the game playing without having to directly control it myself.

Claude proved reasonably competent at prompting OpenAI's image models to generate sprites. You can browse the v2 sprites in the public/assets/sprites folder.

v3: varied terrain

It still wasn't much fun, and the graphics were boring. It was now October, and I had upgraded to Claude Opus 5.5. I told it:

Massively improve this game. Make the graphics and gameplay better (keep it mobile friendly). Render new graphics using the latest OpenAI GPT image API (lookup details) with the API key in the environment variable. Add new unit types and balance the gameplay better. Also add new buildings and better, more varied terrain.

This resulted in five new maps with generated background tiles in a variety of styles, visible here. Opus also regenerated the sprites, making them much more visually appealing. You can try v3 here - it looks like this:

This is starting to feel like a real game! It still wasn't very fun to play though - I found myself getting bored pretty quickly.

v4: the fun update

So far my Battle Drones experiment was confirming my previous belief that coding agents can build a thing that looks like a game but can't actually make something that's genuinely compelling to play.

I shared this theory with someone over dinner, and then thought to myself that I should give the models a proper chance to prove me wrong. I prompted Opus 5.5 on my phone:

This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun.

This time I was running in Ultracode mode, where Claude Code (in this case Claude Code for Web) runs "dynamic workflows", described in their docs as:

A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that orchestrates many subagents at once.

This kicked off many hours of work. I started it in the evening and didn't get a playable result back until late into the next morning. But the results were spectacular.

You can try v4 here - it looks like this:

I had Claude write its own release notes - here are the highlights:

Every skirmish and Daily Op now opens with a choice, gives the side that's losing a way back, and pulls the armies into the middle of the map. There are also two new ways to play.

  • Openers: pick Blitz, Industry or Air Wing before the clock starts.
  • Call-down powers: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod and the Sky Hammer orbital strike.
  • Objectives and salvage: Uplink relays, supply drops and wrecks worth scrap.
  • Feel: combat juice, adaptive music, unit voices and an announcer.
  • Command: battle alerts, game speed, saved squads and touch placement.
  • New modes: Last Stand survival waves and an 8-mission Ops campaign.
  • Progression: heroes, an after-action report with awards, a career, 7 mutators and a Daily Op.

Fights run longer and swing more. In 1,200 AI-vs-AI test matches on Normal, games still undecided after 25 minutes fell from 14% to 0.9%. The share of wins by a side that had been 800+ scrap behind rose from 24% to 46%.

Part of the reason Claude took so long was that it ran over a thousand simulated playtest sessions, and used the results to rebalance the existing units, add new ones, and introduce new features.

v5: Battle Drones goes 3D

After the success of Ultracode at "Make it a LOT more fun", I decided to be more ambitious:

Port this game to three.js with 3D models for all of the buildings and vehicles and landscapes

That was another overnight run. I woke up to this v5 version:

The new 3D models were entirely constructed by Claude in TypeScript code.

v6 (play v6 here) added some more visual polish. v7 (play v7) added robot infantry (troopers, rocket squads, snipers) and a "Condor" troop carrying aircraft.

v8: Archipelago

I was beginning to feel guilty at how little actual design input I had into the game - it really had been a case of me saying "make it more fun" and "add visual polish" for the past few releases.

I'd noticed that the AI didn't use the new infantry and troop carrying aircraft from v7 very often - there wasn't a great strategic reason to use them.

It would be neat if we had a new map with a new game mechanic that actively encouraged players to load up Condors with infantry robots and send them out into the map.

This resulted in my longest prompt yet:

Design a new map. Goal is to make different strategic incentives that encourage use of Infantry and Condors and aerial vehicles.

To do this the map will have limited harvester resources but several more uplinks - but uplinks will be on islands that are inaccessible by land vehicles or infantry. These uplinks can also not be claimed using air vehicles. The ONLY way to get them is to fly infantry there in a Condor.

Armies always start with a Condor and a single squad. If an army has no Condor a new one will be provided for free, flying in from the edge closest to their HQ and landing there. That free condor will come with a single free squad on board.

The two HQs should be entirely separated by water, but still accessible by vehicles thanks to two bridges across the map in different places

I want to encourage a battle over uplinks.

The map should be the times the size of other maps - still square

First research and then critique this design. Only build after we have agreed on any modifications

You get to design a new biome for this

The result was the tropical Archipelago map, with seven island uplinks that players can only capture by flying out infantry in a Condor. It's definitely the most fun map to play, once you've got the hang of the basic game mechanics from the simpler maps. The v9 edition made that map a little more interesting - it now looks like this:

v10: Goliath, and agent battles

I decided to add giant robot mechs to the game - think Jaegers from Pacific Rim, or Titans from Warhammer 40,000.

Here are some of the prompts I used to brainstorm with Claude:

Help me brainstorm ideas for adding giant robots to this game - think dreadnoughts or titans from W20K - how could we do this in a way that enhanced gameplay, kept things balanced, added unique twist? Don't overthink this yet

Let's keep brainstorming. I like the idea that it's a mobile base - that can accept harvested scrap and can have buildings built near it (even if it later moves on) and can produce infantry units too. An interaction with condor would be neat but I don't know what that could be.

Idea: as it gets damage it loses the ability to fire some weapons - by default it has eye laser (like lancers) and arm canons (like titan) and two shoulder mounted mortars, plus machine guns similar to a squad of troops

Damage knocks out mortars and then laser - it always has guns. You can't build next to a building that was only put there because of the mech, you need the mech there for off-base building and only within three squares of it

[...] Lets do two condors can carry the mech

The end result is really cool.

Goliaths can be constructed using a Gantry - a building that can only be created after first building a Fab, Bay, Airpad, and Tech Lab. You can see the Goliath under construction, and it then walks out from the Gantry and can march around the map.

Goliaths can "anchor", which digs them into the ground. In their anchored state they can act as a new HQ, constructing infantry units and additional buildings in a new area.

Two Condor aircraft can hook onto a Goliath, at which point it can be flown around the map!

The game now ends when you destroy the enemy's HQ building and any Goliaths they might have built.

There are also a couple of mutators relating to Goliaths:

  • Goliath Armada starts each side with four airborne Goliaths (each with a pair of Condors) and no other units.
  • Robot Love adds a special rule: if enemy Goliaths get close to each other on the battlefield they fall in love and the game ends in a draw. (Thank Natalie for that one).

Agent battles

The other v10 feature is agent battles. In musing about how multiplayer could work I had an idea: what if different LLMs could fight it out in the game?

Fun extra challenge: think about how we might make multiplayer available to coding agents. It would be neat if we could set up a battle between eg GPT-6 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 where each model has access to a tool which gives them information about the game (presumably non-visual, but only the information they could see through fog of war etc) and lets them control their units etc [...]

Consult ~/dev/llm/docs and include notes in that file about how LLM could be used here via a new tools plugin

Opus 5.5 went to work on this, producing this AGENT-BATTLES.md proposal and then implementing and testing it. The feature also includes the ability to record and replay these battles - here's a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna, and here's that same battle in a separate debug tool that shows the underlying prompt responses.

The prompt that drives agent battles can be seen here.

There are a few more replays like this linked in the README. I hope to turn this into a full league table at some point in the future.

v11: Random Maps

This version exists purely because I glanced at my Claude Usage page one day and saw that I'd only used 75% of my weekly allowance and it was resetting in 45 minutes. I decided to see if I could get an extra Battle Drones feature from my remaining tokens, and picked "random map" as the target:

Design and implement a mechanism for generating a random map using any of the available biomes - it should be the size of the largest map and rivers and bridges and rocks and forest and scrap and crystals are all in play. Make them rotationally symmetric and use a seed to allow them to be selected or reused later. You have 45 minutes to build this! Be creative.

Here's the transcript, and an image Claude generated to show me its work:

v12: Multiplayer via sound

I only just got this working, so I've not had much time to actively test it yet. The latest Battle Drones now supports multiplayer via two devices sat within microphone distance of each other!

This feature started out as my Chirp Pong experiment from last week. I pointed Claude Code at that working proof of concept:

Clone Simonw/tools from GitHub and look at recent branches for the example pong game that uses web microphone to implement multiplayer between two phones via audio signals

Build a version of that for battledrones

Opus built this Radio Probe tool to measure how much bandwidth we could get between two devices and, based on positive results from that, implemented a full audio modem system. I've tried it between laptops, iPhones and iPads so far and it seems to work really well!

Why use sound for this? Because I love static HTML that costs nothing to run, and I don't want to spin up a server somewhere and then stay responsible for keeping it operating for as long as anyone might want to play the game.

Some thoughts

I know almost nothing about game development. This makes it a great opportunity to try out coding agents in a field where my existing software engineering experience has less impact on the results.

Games are also super low stakes. The worst that can happen is one of my silly game experiments suffers a bug.

This morning (via Hacker News) I found Steam Fans Are Begging for a No-AI Filter as Steam Next Fest Is Filled With Slop. I wouldn't personally dream of submitting Battle Drones to an event like this - it's still way too low effort to warrant consideration as a legitimate indie gaming project.

... but I can now see a path to vibe coded games like this being taken seriously. Battle Drones is fun, it looks good, it has innovative features (the multiplayer-over-audio thing is a first for an RTS as far as I can tell).

I'd love to see what someone with better taste than me and a driving passion to produce something truly exceptional could build!

A few other observations from this project:

  • Static HTML and JavaScript is a fantastic medium for games development. WebGL works great, and Three.js (and Phaser before it) are excellent platforms to build on that the current models know inside out.
  • This also lets them run as Progressive Web Apps - I didn't ask for it, but Battle Drones works offline. I was able to play it on a plane despite never having directly installed it - my phone had it cached.
  • Giving Claude an OpenAI API key and telling it to generate images using OpenAI's models works really well. It can view the images it has generated and iterate on the prompts.
  • Opus 5.5 is spectacular at 3D modeling using Three.js (and Blender, and no doubt other 3D applications as well). The same is true of GPT-6 Astra. They are absolutely capable of building models for 3D game projects.
  • For features like replay and multiplayer it's useful to have a deterministic simulation engine. At one point Claude had to replace calls to Math.sin() and Math.cos() and friends with custom versions because different browsers (Chrome vs. Safari, for example) returned very slightly different numbers, desynchronizing the replay.
  • Opus 5.5 can write music! There are no audio files in this project - the soundtrack is entirely generated through code, varies across different maps, and even gets more intense as the battle heats up. See Scrimshaw Jukebox for a previous experiment with Claude for music composition.
  • I still can't get over how well the prompt "Make it a LOT more fun" worked.
  • Tools are effectively free. I prompted up the Radio Probe, the Model browser, the Agent vs. Agent debug tool, and Claude Code built a bunch of tools for itself that I haven't even explored myself.
  • Audio-based multiplayer between static HTML games works! I hope to see a whole lot more games use this same pattern - in digging around today I've not found much prior art beyond Siner by Alon Horesh and ggwave by Georgi Gerganov (also of llama.cpp fame).
  • Claude Code "Ultracode" burns tokens like there's no tomorrow, but it can also solve complex problems (like adding audio-based multiplayer) from a single prompt.
  • I'm still not quite over the guilt of building software in this way. I don't feel like I've earned the right to create something this good, in a field in which I have so little prior experience! At this point I've shown it to enough people in private that it felt wrong not to publish it for everyone else to see and learn from.

entry.title: The Best Monopoly Strategy, Tested on 300 Million Games
entry.summary:
Perfect Play ran over 300 million games of Monopoly to determine the best strategy and the most common mistakes players make. I turned eight classic Monopoly strategies into computer players and made them play 312,898,560 games against each other. At a table of four, the best one won 43% of its games. The worst one won 3%. The gap doesn’t come from one clever trick. It comes from four common mistakes: being picky about what you buy, saving your cash, stopping at three houses, and refusing to trade. Then I let the computer tune every habit at once, to see how far a carefully tuned player can go and which color set is really worth fighting for.
P.S. entry.title: How Japanese Dried Bonito Is Made
entry.summary:
This workshop founded in 1882 still makes dried bonito like they did back in the Edo period. How katsuobushi — Japanese dried bonito, said to be the world’s hardest food — is made in Nishi-Izu, Japan. Inside Kanesa Katsuobushi Shoten, a workshop founded in 1882, 5th-generation craftsman Yasuhisa Serizawa still uses the 200-year-old “tebiyama” hand-fired smoke-drying method that only a few workshops in Japan preserve. Watch fresh bonito being filleted and boiled for 90 minutes, smoke-dried more than 10 times over a hand-tended wood fire, repaired with bonito paste, fermented with koji mold and sun-dried for months — over half a year until the fish becomes as hard as wood and shines like a jewel. From fresh catch to katsuobushi.
Check out Kanesa Katsuobushi Shoten’s website for more info; here’s what they say about the tebiyama drying/smoking method (Google translation): This method of making dried bonito flakes has been used in the Tago district of West Izu for a long time, and its history is said to date back about 300 years (to the Edo period). It involves digging a vertical hole about 2 meters deep, burning firewood (raw wood from Izu: oak, sawtooth oak, cherry, etc.) from the bottom of the hole, and smoking and drying the dried bonito flakes with the high temperature of an open flame. This method is called the Tebiyama-shiki smoking method. It is the oldest existing smoking method, and only a few bonito flake manufacturers in the country continue to use this method to make dried bonito flakes, so it is said to be a legendary method. The Tebiyama-shiki smoking method is said to produce dried bonito flakes with a rich flavor because the surface of the bonito is smoked all at once with the high temperature of an open flame, locking in the umami.
(thx, caroline)

entry.title: A Tiny 24 FPS E-Ink Game Boy Emulator
entry.summary:
This is really impressive: a software engineer got a Game Boy emulator running at 30 fps on a tiny e-ink screen. If you’re familiar with e-paper, you know that they normally refresh much slower (2-3 times a second), not nearly quick enough to play even a simple video game. This guy wrote his own display driver that got the refresh rate up to 30 times per second. From the transcript of the video explaining how e-paper works and how he hacked the display to make it play games: Unlike conventional displays like LCD or OLED, ePaper stores its image physically using charged black and white pigment particles. By changing the electric field, the display moves the pigments towards or away from the surface, which in the end gives us black- or white-looking pixel. And usually a sequence of several electrical pulses called a waveform is needed to move the pigment back and forth, before finally driving it towards the new image. This helps produce a clean result without leaving too much of the previous image behind. But this takes a lot of time.
The project is open source — you can get the plans and code on GitHub. This engineer was inspired by Wenting Zhang’s e-paper Game Boy emulator:

This research task is really an experiment in running Claude Code for web in "Ultracode" mode, as described in Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows in the Claude Code documentation.

With Ultracode turned on, Claude Code makes aggressive use of dynamic workflows - it generates JavaScript that defines and coordinates a network of subagents to take on complex problems.

My initial prompt was this - I meant "hit the rows directly", the word "delete" was an accidental typo on my phone:

Write a SQLite extension in Rust that implants SPARQL and runs really fast because it can hit the delete rows directly

This caused Claude Code for web to churn for over 12 hours. I checked in on its progress the next day and sent a single follow-up prompt when I noticed how many Rust crates it had built:

Every folder in the crates/ directory needs a README

Include a tutorial.md teaching users how to install the extension and how to run it in the SQLite CLI and then teaching them SPARQL in addition to how to use the SQLite extension

Include a script with the tutorial for populating a SQLite database with useful and realistic example data for that tutorial

This project feels like next-level vibe coding - it's not remotely feasible to review the code that was produced here, and even following the documentation is a significant investment in work. entry.title: How Hunting Owls Use Sound to “See” Under the Snow
entry.summary:
The great grey owl basically has a sound cone for a face, which helps it hunt down voles burrowing through snow in the winter. The owl’s large facial ruff, formed of dense feathers, helps amplify sound and funnel it towards his ears. Through half a meter of snow, the sound of scampering feet is inaudible to us. The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones.

entry.title: LaTeX renderer

Tool: LaTeX renderer

Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app Tiny Little Office, which provides a suite of web app content editors (a Word Processor, Outliner, Presentation Builder, Spreadsheet, Calculator, Drawing Tool, Diagram Maker, Animator, Calendar, and Trip Planner).

Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the #fragment section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link.

It also has an llms.txt file telling agents how to construct URLs that will render as documents. Claude used that file to generate this link to a deck that explains how the URL format works:

Tiny Little Office inspired me to have Claude Code (Opus 5.5 Extra) build a similar tool that works with LaTeX. Here's the sequence of prompts I used:

I want a tool where you can link to it with a fragment hash #code-here and it treats that code as LaTeX and renders it really effectively. It should also support a prefix which means the latex is compressed with a custom compression dictionary optimized for latex. Use the best available latex render library from a CDN (consider WebAssembly too). If loaded without a fragment hash show an editor you can paste latex into and then toggle to a "rendered" view. That rendered view should be bookmarkable. The #fragment view should let you switch to edit source too.

Since it was working in my tools repo I told it to take inspiration from the <iframe sandbox="..."> mechanism used by my existing SVG in Markdown tool as protection against XSS risks:

Safe from XSS? We could run in an iframe sandbox like we do on the SVG markdown render project

I had it copy the Gist/URL loading feature from that tool as well:

We should have an option to load latex from a URL (or gist) similar to the markdown SVG tool

Here's an example link. The tool uses Pako 2.1.0, MathJax 4.1.3, faster-latex 0.3.1, and DOMPurify 3.4.16.

entry.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
entry.summary:
Redesigning source control at Anthropic

Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months.

In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day.

They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart (code here) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026:

This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity.

"Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. They had some pretty extreme requirements:

The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.

The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months.

As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that:

Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns.

Via Hacker News

I added support to llm-gemini for the new Gemini 4 Argon model, made available today via the Gemini API and for customers of their $100/month subscription plan.

Here are the low, medium and high pelicans. As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their staff have invested in SVG specifically (and who have boasted about their pelicans before.)

Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents:

The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.

But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5.

Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness.

One useful clue for that comes from Artificial Analysis, who publish the total cost to run their benchmark using each model. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models.

When the price doubles it will still be a little cheaper than GPT-6 Astra.

entry.title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
entry.summary:
Python 3.15 is here! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11.

First, some highlights from Python 3.15.

Explicit lazy imports

I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810. These let you import modules like so:

lazy import json
lazy from pathlib import Path

The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows.

My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost.

Unpacking in comprehensions

The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation:

lists = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]
[*L for L in lists]
# [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
# equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L]

sets = [{1, 2}, {2, 3}, {3, 4}]
{*s for s in sets}
# {1, 2, 3, 4}
# equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s}

dicts = [{'a': 1}, {'b': 2}, {'a': 3}]
{**d for d in dicts}
# {'a': 3, 'b': 2}
# equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()}

PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448, which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015.

A sampling profiler

Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing, and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling.

Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They're very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first.

I've previously used tools like py-spy for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library.

If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use sudo on macOS):

sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234

Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this:

It can also produce flame graphs like this and heat maps like this, and can even output a format that can be viewed in the Firefox profiler UI.

3.15 isn't much faster than 3.14

Miguel Grinberg investigated How fast is Python 3.15? the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase.

Miguel's explorations of 3.14 last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories.

Upgrading to Python 3.15 with uv

I used the following sequence of commands to get uv to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade uv itself to ensure it knew about the new release:

uv self update

Then I installed the stable 3.15 release:

uv python install 3.15

And told uv that I wanted that to be the default for every uv run command, unless the project itself pinned a different version:

uv python pin --global 3.15

Now the following reports 3.15 as the version:

uv run python --version

I already have a bunch of tools installed using uv tool install. I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this:

uv tool upgrade datasette --python 3.15

Then I can confirm the version like this:

datasette --get /-/versions.json | jq

Highlights from Python 3.11

The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported.

My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11.

Here's the What's new in Python 3.11 document. I finally get to rely on tomllib being available!

Datasette makes extensive use of asyncio. 3.11 adds TaskGroup and timeout(), and several more new features.

datetime.UTC is a new in 3.11 alias for datetime.timezone.utc.

Python's SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including:

  • setlimit() and getlimit() expose a mechanism for setting SQLite runtime limits from Python.
  • create_window_function() lets us create custom window functions in Python, as a class with step(), value(), inverse(), and finalize() methods.
  • blobopen() provides an efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of large BLOB binary values stored in a SQLite row.
  • You can now call set_authorizer(None) to remove a SQLite authorizer. Datasette had a workaround for this!

Plus a whole bunch of improvements to Python's typing system.

I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here's my first Datasette PR removing that set_authorizer(None) workaround.

I've also updated my click-app, datasette-plugin, python-lib, and llm-plugin cookiecutter templates to test against Python 3.11 through Python 3.15.

entry.title: Dwarf Fortress uses version control now
entry.summary:
I remember hearing a while ago that Dwarf Fortress didn't use version control. That fact has been lodged in my head, because given its inherent complexity I have trouble imagining a codebase that would benefit from version control more. That's art.

I went looking and I'm sad to report that the days without version control appear to have ended. Quoting Tarn Adams over time:

  • March 2013: "I don't use version control -- I didn't like the feeling of having the code get committed into a black box thingy with no immediate upside"
  • March 2016: "I don’t even use version control. If you don’t know what that is then you’re not gonna yell at me. If you even know what version control is you’re gonna be like, ‘You don’t use version control? You don’t use source control? What is wrong with you? How can you even work? I’m just not cut out for it, in a sense. It’s been 15 years, so the reasons have change over time, but that’s my current understanding of it." 
  • March 2023: "I've got Discord channels to check and version control stuff to use now, so the process is definitely a little more involved"

That March 2023 quote comes from an interview about the release on Steam which made them millionaires. I'm a tiny bit sad that they gave in before they hit that milestone, but what an impressive run.

entry.title: Deno is joining Cloudflare
entry.summary:
Deno is joining Cloudflare

The Deno team released the first version of celld back in August - their open source implementation of the Durable Objects pattern from Cloudflare Workers.

Today, Cloudflare are acquiring Deno outright, with the goal of building on celld to "make workerd self-hosting a first-class supported way to build and run apps using the Workers programming model" (see the Cloudflare blog.)

The bad news is that Deno itself will not be maintained by Cloudflare beyond the next year:

We will support the Deno runtime for another year with monthly releases containing bug fixes and security updates. After that year we will end our development of the Deno runtime. Deno will remain open source, and we welcome others who want to continue its development.

Deno (and Node.js) creator Ryan Dahl explained that decision in a comment on Hacker News:

It's a joint decision and I agree with it. I'm most invested in its success and have put the most work into it - and I no longer think it's where I can do the most important work. There are some good ideas in Deno and it's well engineered - but it ultimately is not solving big problems. It has been sucked into the gravity well of node compatibility, which forces it to behave exactly as Node does. Why reimplement Node? It works. Marginal performance or UX or security benefits are not enough.

I'm interested in building powerful new abstractions. celld has been working remarkably well, depending only on object storage for coordination and persistence. It is not just a slightly different API to interact with the file system or network - it's an entirely new model for server development.

My favorite feature of Deno has long been the permissions system, where you can run a Deno script and specify exactly which files and folders it can read and write to, and which network hosts it can access.

Node.js has a similar permissions model these days, added in Node v20.0.0 in April 2023 and declared stable in Node v22.13.0 in January 2025. They don't yet support allow-listing specific network hosts though - networking is either on or off.

Via Hacker News

It might be that this text-only quiz game from 1993 is the most challenging F1 video game of all time. Here are a couple of the 23 questions from Gerhard Berger’s Formula 1 Quiz: 3. Which team was the best in the 80’s? Statistically, it’s McLaren, but that’s not a correct answer. The correct answer is “Mc Laren.” 4. Who is the youngest champion of ever? The correct answer in 1993 was Emerson Fittipaldi, but his full name cannot be accepted because it contains too many characters for the computer. The game will not take “Fittipaldi,” “Emerson,” or “E Fittipaldi.” The answer must be “Fit.” The real quiz, it soon becomes clear, is not a test of one’s F1 knowledge, but figuring out what the game expects to hear.
Berger is a former F1 driver, and the game is so weird and forgotten that it’s not even listed on his Wikipedia page — and it might not have been an official game at all. What is listed on his Wikipedia page is the epic prank war he waged against teammate Ayrton Senna: In an Australian hotel room, Berger filled Senna’s bed with frogs. An infuriated Senna confronted Berger, who replied, “Did you find the snake?” Senna retaliated by putting strong-smelling French cheese in the air conditioning unit of Berger’s room.
It seems likely it was in this spirit that Gerhard Berger’s Formula 1 Quiz game was created: as a prank Berger himself would have enjoyed. entry.title: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice
entry.summary:
I shipped a new feature for my blog today: the Newsletters page, which offers an index of all of the newsletters I've sent out, both my free weekly Substack and my monthly sponsors-only updates. I built the feature almost entirely using my voice, chatting away to my laptop while I cooked dinner.

Codex voice mode

I used the ChatGPT desktop app for this, in the Codex tab, using the voice conversation mode, running against a local development environment. Here's what that looks like:

I started the session against my local simonwillisonblog checkout by typing:

Start dev server and open in browser

This gave me a preview of the site that it would be working on, and meant that I could later ask it to show me the new pages so I could visually track its progress.

Then I clicked the "Start new voice chat" button - that's not the microphone button, it's the one to the right of it - and set my laptop up in the kitchen so I could talk to it while I cooked.

Talking to my computer

I had a pretty good idea of what I wanted to build, and it's a simple enough Django feature that I was certain the model (in this case GPT-6 Astra High) would be able to do it. A new model, a migration, some view code, templates, and a couple of import functions to populate the database from external sources.

Here's an extract of my voice transcript that was captured by Codex:

Um, they do not. Um, this is going to be a new type of content. Um, it's not going to show up... Oh, hold on. Yeah, no- I do not want this to show up in my, um, tag pages and date archive pages and... Actually, no, I think... I don't want it on the tag pages. I don't want it on the, um, blog index page. But I think I do want it to show up on the date-based pages. You know, if you navigate to September the 19th, and I sent a newsletter on that page, I think I want that to show up. So... this is- so I think we probably need a new model. The other thing is that I want them searchable, uh the Substack ones are not searchable, because those are actually just copies of other s- on content on my blog. These monthly ones do contain unique content, and spe- and once they're... published, like once they're made public a month after they've gone out, I want them to show up on my search results.

Apparently this was clear enough that the model knew what I wanted to build! You can read the full transcript, disfluencies and all, in this Gist.

We went on like this for about half an hour (the time it took to cook dinner). The model would reply and occasionally ask clarifying questions, then get to work modifying the code.

What we built

We got a surprisingly long way entirely by voice:

  • A new model and migration to represent imported newsletters in Django, plus Django Admin configuration for that
  • Four working imports:
    • The most recent Substack items via RSS
    • Every other Substack item via their undocumented API, which GPT-6 Astra knew about (it tried /api/v1/archive directly) and then ran a search to figure out how to paginate it and found this article by Karen Spinner
    • All of my published monthly newsletters from my simonw/monthly-newsletter-archive GitHub repository
    • My most recent private sponsors-only newsletter from a private repository
  • The /newsletters/ and /newsletters/2026/ public archive pages
  • Newsletters showing up on day and month archive pages too, but not on tag pages or my homepage
  • Weekly Substack newsletters link to Substack; archived monthly newsletters have their own pages
  • Integration with my site search engine

It was almost ready to ship. The catch was the imports: Astra offered to export data from my local copy so I could import that into production, but I wanted it to work like my other import scripts. Since some of the data lived in a private GitHub repository, this would involve creating a new API key, and for that I knew I'd have to sit at the keyboard for a while.

Finishing it with a review

Once I had finished cooking and judged it mostly feature-complete, I had Codex create a branch and open a pull request.

I reviewed the code in the GitHub PR interface. It was nearly what I needed, except it had chosen to use Git in a subprocess for one of the import scripts. I needed one of the imports to pull from a private Git repository, so I figured the API would be a better bet. I switched to typing and had Codex swap that out for an API-based import instead.

You can see the changes I made during the review in the extra commits on the PR. I fixed the import mechanism and made a few tweaks to the display of those public pages. It took an additional half hour of typing-based prompting to get to the point where I was happy to deploy it to production by landing the PR.

The end result

You can see the end result at the new newsletters index page, or view the page for a previous monthly newsletter.

The index page shows my most recent Substack weekly newsletters and GitHub sponsors monthly newsletters mixed together in reverse chronological order. Further down the page are links to my by-year archive pages.

GPT-6 Astra designed the page, and then tweaked that design based on my vocal feedback from glancing at the local preview across the kitchen.

Better for multi-tasking than as a daily driver

OpenAI love using voice-driven demos like this one for things like DevDay - and they do work well in that environment. I don't think this is going to be a daily driver for me though.

I've written before about how much "work" I get done using ChatGPT voice mode on my phone while walking the dog - mostly research and brainstorming, but occasionally actual development work by having ChatGPT write and test out snippets of code.

This feels different. The addition of the visual preview, plus being able to type or paste things in via the keyboard when I need to communicate something that doesn't work vocally, makes this a much more powerful way of interacting with a coding agent.

I still switch back to typing once I get down to the details of things though. Being able to paste in examples and error messages, or directly highlight the code or feature that needs changing, remains more efficient than trying to describe it in words.

I mainly work from home, which is good because there's no way I'd want to talk to my computer like this in a shared workspace!

The killer feature for me is the ability to multi-task. I usually cook with a podcast or TikTok running; now I can actually build stuff instead.

entry.title: ttok 1.0
entry.summary:
Release: ttok 1.0

I released ttok 0.4, ran uv tool upgrade ttok, piped a file into the new version... and realized that it was defaulting to the GPT-4 tokenizer when it should very clearly default to GPT-5/GPT-6 instead!

I figured switching the default was a reasonable excuse to finally ship a 1.0.

OpenAI haven't actually confirmed that GPT-6 uses the same tokenizer as the GPT-5 family yet - there's an angry issue about it - but I found this commit by William Liu which reports on an experiment he ran confirming that the tokenizers are likely the same:

All seven GPT models (5.5, 5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna, 6 Astra/Sol/Luna) report 44,794 tokens and match each other on every one of the 31 fixtures. GPT-6 introduces no input-count change on this corpus.

entry.title: Claude Haiku 5.5
entry.summary:
As previously promised, here's Anthropic's new fast, low cost model: Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5.

The previous Haiku, 4.5, was very much showing its age. It came out almost a year ago, and was priced at $1/million input and $5/million output - relatively expensive even back then, and a full 10x the price of OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna, released last month.

The new Haiku exactly matches the price of GPT-6 Luna - $0.10/$0.50 - up to 100,000 tokens. Beyond 100,000 tokens the price increases 5x to $0.50/$2.50. Luna itself has a price increase at 272,000 tokens but only to $0.20/$0.75.

Haiku 5.5 also uses a new, less generous tokenizer. My Claude Token Counter tool shows that the same long prompt uses around 1.25x as many tokens with Haiku 5.5 compared to Haiku 4.5, so there's a hidden price increase there.

If your workloads fit in 100,000 tokens, Haiku is the same price as Luna and reports higher benchmark scores. Above 100,000 tokens, Luna looks like a much better deal.

The most recent release of llm-anthropic finally fixed it so I don't need to ship a new version of that plugin for every new model. I tested the new model like this:

llm install -U llm-anthropic
llm anthropic refresh
llm -m claude-haiku-5.5 "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" -o thinking_effort low

Pelicans

Here are pelicans for low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. The new Haiku doesn't let you disable reasoning, and defaults to medium. I got a good bicycle frame for everything beyond low. The low effort pelican cost 0.0936 cents and took 7 seconds.

This max effort pelican took 5 minutes 9 seconds to generate, but still only cost me 3.3826 cents:

For comparison, here's the pelican I got a year ago from Haiku 4.5 (for 0.7583 cents - Haiku 4.5 did not support reasoning levels). It sucked at drawing pelicans:

And a generous API credit scheme for subscribers

In addition to Haiku 5.5, Anthropic announced today that they are halving the price of cache reads for Sonnet 5.5. They've also added API credits to subscription plans:

Second, this week, we’ll roll out a new monthly API credit to all Max and Team subscribers for use on the Claude Platform. Max 5x users will get $100 in credits per month, Max 20x users will get $200, and Team subscribers will receive up to $500, pooled across their users.

Claiming this is pleasantly easy: navigate to Settings -> Billing and select the API organization that should benefit from the credits every month:

The API credits exactly match the cost of the subscription itself. This is really generous - it makes it much easier for subscribers to use the API. Anthropic also let you disable auto-reload for the API, with the consequence that "API requests will stop when your balance runs out" - exactly what you want if you're planning to burn through those API credits without risk of a nasty billing surprise.

Note that the monthly credits do not roll over - use them or lose them.

OpenAI still allow you to use your Codex subscription for personal API use, which works out as a better deal for heavy API users. This new credit scheme goes at least some way to overcoming that difference.

entry.title: EmbeddingGemma 2
entry.summary:
My comment on EmbeddingGemma 2 — Hacker News.

I really appreciate that EmbeddingGemma 2 is under the Apache 2.0 license.

For embedding models in particular, I don't think it makes sense to use a closed, proprietary, hosted-only model.

Most applications of embedding models involve calculating thousands or even millions of embedding vectors and storing them for later comparison.

If your model is proprietary, the vendor is likely someday going to decide to stop offering that model. They'll have a better model to replace it, but you still need to pay to re-calculate those millions of stored existing vectors.

(In April 2024 OpenAI offered to "cover the financial cost of users re-embedding content with these new models" - https://openai.com/index/gpt-4-api-general-availability/ - but I don't think that's something we can rely on from every provider.)

Notably, I don't want to host the model myself. I'd much rather pay a provider for a hosted model while knowing that if they ever stop hosting it I can run the open weights version myself - or find another vendor who can do that for me.

entry.title: We're going to need default hard budget caps on pretty much everything
entry.summary:
Here's a product feature which the world is going to need a whole lot more of over the coming months and years: default hard budget caps. I'm talking about the feature of pay-by-usage services and APIs that lets you say "after $X/month, cut this thing off and return errors". These need to be hard limits. Soft caps, "after $X/month, send me a warning email", will not cut it.

Coding agents, and personal agents (coding agents wrapped in a less threatening UI), greatly reduce the friction of spinning up code that can do useful things. Sometimes those things cost money - calls to paid APIs, or hosted web applications, or systems that can bill for additional storage and compute.

Nobody wants to wake up to an email sent at midnight warning about a budget limit and find that, while they slept, their rogue service had consumed several hundred (or several thousand) more dollars of usage.

An argument against this is that businesses don't want their hosted applications to start throwing errors because some budget was exceeded. I expect that most businesses and individuals would prefer errors to a surprise $10,000+ bill.

I think hard budget caps need to be the default. If someone wants to live dangerously they should be able to do that, but it needs to be on an opt-in basis. Have a nice, clear checkbox somewhere prominent:

Remove the budget cap. My application will not be shut down if I exceed the configured budget limit, and I will be responsible for subsequent charges.

The service I most want to see this from is AWS. I've heard plenty of stories from people who refuse to use AWS for personal projects out of (justified) fear that a runaway service might bankrupt them. I've also heard stories from people who didn't anticipate this and ended up seriously burned.

... and it turns out AWS finally launched spending limits a few weeks ago! From their announcement New AWS experience helps builders get started and ship faster on 16th September:

When you're ready to upgrade to a paid plan, you can set a monthly spend limit for your project based on your usage patterns so that you stay within your budget. If a project's usage reaches its spend limit, your project is paused for that month.

See also Create a spend limit in AWS Settings, though that page warns that "We're currently releasing our new experience to a limited number of customers." Here's hoping that hits general availability for existing accounts soon.

Google Cloud launched a similar feature in July, called Spend Caps, which lets you "set a monthly financial cap on specific services within a project". Looks like this is becoming a trend!

In an ideal world, our agents could help with this. It would be great if agents started biasing towards recommending providers with hard budget caps, and warning new and inexperienced builders against deploying applications using uncapped services that might get them into trouble.

entry.title: Ozymandias, by Percy Bysshe Shelley
entry.summary: Can you please translate the Shelley poem “Ozymandias” into ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English? Copilot said: Certainly. Since “Ozymandias” is in the public domain, it can be adapted freely. ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English aims for short sentences, one meaning per sentence, controlled vocabulary, and minimal figurative language. The result loses much of the poem’s beauty, but preserves its information and message. Ozymandias in ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English I met a traveller from an old country. The traveller gave a report. He said: “In a desert, there are two large stone legs. The legs stand upright. The rest of the statue is not present. Near the legs, there is a stone head on the ground. The face has a frown. The mouth shows contempt. The expression shows authority. The sculptor understood the character of the ruler. The sculptor made these features in the stone. The ruler is dead. The sculptor and the ruler are dead. The stone still shows these features. On the base of the statue, there is an inscription. The inscription says: ‘I am Ozymandias. I am king of kings. Powerful rulers must look at my works. They must feel despair because they cannot equal them.’ No works remain. The statue is damaged. The area around it is empty. There is only flat desert. The sand extends a long distance in all directions.” Notes on the conversion Metaphors and poetic imagery are replaced with direct statements. Emotional language is reduced to observable facts. Ambiguity is removed where possible. The central message remains: a powerful ruler tried to create a permanent monument, but time destroyed almost everything, and his power is gone. In a sense, converting Ozymandias into ASD-STE100 turns it from a Romantic poem into something that reads like a field inspection report on the failure of long-term brand preservation.

entry.title: Prince Was One of the First Players of The Oregon Trail
entry.summary:
In this video, Patrick Hicks tells the story of the development of the classic educational video game The Oregon Trail and how Prince (you know, the genius musical artist) was one of the first people in the world to play the very first version of the game. The basic story is that a college history major (Don Rawitsch) teamed up with two friends (Bill Heinemann and Paul Dillenberger), both of whom were math majors and had some programming experience, to make a computer game to liven up the history class that Rawitsch was student teaching. While developing the game, Heinemann & Dillenberger tested it out with some kids at the high school at which they were student teaching…and one of those kids was Prince Rogers Nelson. Paul would later say that he heard about Prince before he even met him. One of the other teachers told him, “There’s this kid here who basically is running his own business. He’s this amazing musician who plays all these instruments and writes his own songs.” And then later, Paul realized that that was Prince.
But listen to Hicks tell the whole thing…it’s a good story. And if you want to hear a lot more of the story, here’s Gaming Historian’s feature-length documentary (the Prince anecdote is at ~24:00).

entry.title: Map of the Lighthouses of the World
entry.summary:
From mapped.earth, a map of every lighthouse on the planet, along with other charted lights like lighted buoys and such. The screenshots above are static but the lights on the real map move: each lighthouse sweeps out its actual arc and the reach of the beams is true to scale. I recorded a short video of how it looks on the site:
Each lighthouse has a unique light characteristic so that ships can tell them apart: In any of these designs an observer, rather than seeing a continuous weak light, sees a brighter light during short time intervals. These instants of bright light are arranged to create a light characteristic or pattern specific to a lighthouse. For example, the Scheveningen Lighthouse flashes are alternately 2.5 and 7.5 seconds. Some lights have sectors of a particular color (usually formed by colored panes in the lantern) to distinguish safe water areas from dangerous shoals. Modern lighthouses often have unique reflectors or racon transponders so the radar signature of the light is also unique.
